items.stem: A charged capacitor in a long-interval RC timer discharges through a fixed 50 kΩ resistor. The linear plot of ln(V / V) against time t passes through the vertical intercept (0 s, 2.351) and the endpoint (50 s, 0.351).
items.workedSolution: (a) taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference. (b) Gradient m = -0.04000 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/m = 25.00 s ≈ 25.0 s. (c) C = τ/R = 500 μF. (d) uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

markScheme.criterion: Shows taking natural logs produces a linear relation between ln(V) and t.
Identifies gradient = −1/τ and vertical intercept = ln(V₀).
Evaluates negative gradient m = -0.0400 s⁻¹ and uses τ = −1/m.
Correct time constant τ = 25.0 s.
Correct capacitance C = τ / R = 500 μF.
States that it uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

parts.prompt: Explain why plotting the natural logarithm of potential difference against time yields a straight line, identifying the physical meaning of its gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: From the exponential discharge equation, taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference.
workingSteps: Take natural logarithms of both sides of the exponential decay equation.
Compare with a linear equation to identify the negative gradient and the vertical intercept.

parts.prompt: Determine the time constant τ of the RC circuit from the gradient of the graph.
workingSteps: Time constant τ = −1 / m = 25.00 s ≈ 25.0 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in μF given R = 50 kΩ.
State why determining τ from the gradient of a ln(V) against t graph is more reliable than drawing an initial tangent to a V against t curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The logarithmic gradient method is more reliable because it uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.
workingSteps: Drawing a tangent to a curve by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise at a single point, whereas a linear best-fit averages random errors over all readings.

items.stem: Examine the 8.0 s velocity–time curve for a solar-powered desert research rover (initial coordinate 22.0 m from the base-camp beacon). What mean speed is achieved during this movement?
items.workedSolution: Distance travelled Δx = ½(8 + 4)(12) = 72.0 m (independent of the 22 m starting offset). Mean speed = 72.0 / 8 = 9.00 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides trapezium distance (72.0 m) by 8 s to obtain 9.00 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Refer to the tensile stress–strain plot for a thermoplastic elastomer tether, whose limit of proportionality lies at strain 0.2. Calculate its initial Young's modulus.
items.workedSolution: Up to the limit of proportionality at ε = 0.2, stress reaches 150 MPa. Young's modulus E = σ / ε = 150 / 0.2 = 750 MPa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial linear gradient E = 150 / 0.2 = 750 MPa (C).

items.stem: In an electrostatics investigation with silvered glass spheres positioned above a digital load pan, F is plotted against r⁻² up to 100.0 m⁻². Extract the proportionality constant k|Q₁Q₂| given by the slope.
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.1 N; at r⁻² = 100 m⁻², F = 1.2 N. Gradient = (1.2 − 0.1) / 100 = 0.0110 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.1 N to get (1.2 − 0.1) / 100 = 0.0110 N m² (A).

items.stem: A student measures the V–I curve shown for a halogen projection bulb. Determine the resistance of the device at I = 2.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 2 A, V = 11 V, so R = 11 / 2 = 5.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 11 / 2 = 5.50 Ω (B).

items.stem: Connecting opposite uncertainty-bar ends at 1.5 mW and 7.5 mW in an optical photodiode irradiance calibration produces the steepest worst-fit line plotted. Find its gradient.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 1.5 mW, y₁ = 3 μA; at x₂ = 7.5 mW, y₂ = 24 μA. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (24 − 3) / (7.5 − 1.5) = 3.50 μA mW⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (24 − 3) / (7.5 − 1.5) = 3.50 μA mW⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: For the sealed dry-air glass bulb plotted with vertical error bars ±1.4 kPa on the suppressed-origin graph, the best-fit gradient is 0.3650 kPa K⁻¹ and the steepest acceptable worst-fit line passing through all error bars has gradient 0.3125 kPa K⁻¹. What is the absolute uncertainty in the gradient?
items.workedSolution: Absolute uncertainty Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = |0.3125 − 0.3650| = 0.05250 kPa K⁻¹ ≈ 0.0525 kPa K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 0.0525 kPa K⁻¹.

items.stem: Using two light gates in a gravitational field g = 9.8 m s⁻², a student records speed v of a levitated neodymium shuttle descending an inclined guide (inclination sin θ = 0.3) after passing an initial gate at s = 0.0 m with speed u₀ > 0, plotting v² against distance s up to 2.5 m. According to v² = u₀² + 2as, what is the gradient Δ(v²) / Δs of the line?
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 3.5 m² s⁻² and at s = 2.5 m, v² = 18.2 m² s⁻². Gradient = (18.2 − 3.5) / 2.5 = 2(9.8)(0.3) = 5.88 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 3.5 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.3) to get 5.88 m s⁻² (A).

items.stem: The displacement–time graph shows an ultrasonic rangefinder target cart moving on an air track from t = 0.0 s to t = 12.0 s. What is its velocity during the initial stage from t = 0.0 s to t = 4.0 s?
items.workedSolution: At t = 0.0 s, s₀ = 6 m; at t = 4 s, s₁ = 26 m. Velocity v = Δs / Δt = (26 − 6) / 4 = 5.00 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts initial position s₀ = 6 m to obtain v = (26 − 6) / 4 = 5.00 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: A student plots current I (y-axis) against potential difference V (x-axis) for a uniform nichrome wire of length 1.20 m and cross-sectional area 6.60 × 10⁻⁸ m². The straight line of best fit passes through the origin and the point (10.0 V, 0.500 A). What is the resistivity of the nichrome?
items.workedSolution: Gradient m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.5000 A / 10.00 V = 0.05000 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 20.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 1.100 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m ≈ 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m.

items.stem: A student calibrates a robotics compliant-joint spring up to 0.8 m compression (plotted below) before releasing it from rest against an unattached 0.6 kg puck on a horizontal air table.

Uses triangular area ½Fx.
Obtains E_p = 28.8 J.

Obtains v = 9.80 m s⁻¹.

options.distractorRationale: Inverts Δt / Δ(ln C) to obtain −1/λ (negative mean lifetime) instead of the gradient −λ.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Assumes ln C drops to zero at t = t_max instead of subtracting the non-zero final ordinate ln C(t_max).

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Computes λ = |Δ(ln C) / Δt| correctly in magnitude but omits the negative sign of the downward semi-log slope.

items.stem: Refer to the signed velocity–time graph for a cable-hauled alpine service car travelling on a straight haulage section. Determine the resultant displacement after 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Velocity reaches zero at t = 7 s. Positive area = 54.0 m and area below the axis has magnitude 10.0 m. Net displacement = 54.0 − 10.0 = 44.0 m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts reverse area (10.0 m) from forward area (54.0 m) to obtain 44.0 m (B).

options.distractorRationale: Multiplies half the difference of terminal speeds by total time, ignoring the piecewise plateau durations.

items.stem: During a 4.0 s stator current pulse, a linear-motor launch shuttle (mass 5.0 kg, initial momentum 15.0 kg m s⁻¹) experiences the force–time profile shown. What is the time-averaged resultant force over the 4.0 s interval?
items.workedSolution: Total impulse J = ½(4 + 2)(35) = 105 N s. Mean force F_mean = J / Δt = 105 / 4 = 26.3 N.

markScheme.criterion: Divides impulse (105 N s) by 4 s to obtain 26.3 N (C).

items.workedSolution: (a) R = V / I = 100.0 Ω ≈ 100 Ω. (b) connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the component and reverse the supply connections for negative readings. (c) conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.

parts.prompt: Calculate the static resistance of the component at the highlighted operating point.
workingSteps: Recall that static resistance at a point is R = V / I (not the inverse of the local tangent).
Substitute V = 3.000 V and I = 0.03000 A to obtain R = 100.0 Ω ≈ 100 Ω.

parts.prompt: Describe the circuit arrangement and experimental procedure used to obtain a complete I–V characteristic safely across positive and negative potential differences.
parts.expectedAnswer: To obtain the full characteristic safely, connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the component and reverse the supply connections for negative readings.
workingSteps: Use a potential divider to vary potential difference smoothly from zero while limiting excessive current with a protective resistor.
Measure current with a series ammeter, potential difference with a parallel voltmeter, and reverse the supply leads for negative polarity.

parts.prompt: Explain the physical shape of the I–V characteristic in terms of charge carriers and resistance.
parts.expectedAnswer: The curve shows that the component conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.
workingSteps: Link the changing ratio of potential difference to current directly to the microscopic conduction mechanism.

items.stem: The graph shows how charge Q and potential difference V vary as a sensor-hold capacitor is charged uniformly from zero up to Q = 3.50 mC at V = 14.0 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates. (b) C = Q / V = 250 μF. (c) Triangular area E = ½ Q V = 0.02450 J ≈ 0.0245 J.

markScheme.criterion: States charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
Correct capacitance 250 μF.
Recognises triangular area E = ½ Q V and converts mC to C.
Correct stored energy 0.0245 J.

Determine the electrical energy stored in the capacitor using the shaded triangular area under the graph.
workingSteps: Because V increases linearly from 0 to V_max as charge builds up, energy stored equals the triangular area E = ½ Q V.

items.stem: Over an interval of 12.0 s, a mine hoist cage (initial velocity 18.0 m s⁻¹ upward) follows the plotted acceleration profile. What velocity does it have when t = 12.0 s?
items.workedSolution: Positive a–t area (0 to 6 s) = 36.0 m s⁻¹; negative area magnitude (6 s to 12 s) = 18.0 m s⁻¹. Net Δv = 36.0 − 18.0 = 18.0 m s⁻¹. Final velocity = 18 + (18.0) = 36.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines net signed area (18.0 m s⁻¹) with u₀ = 18 m s⁻¹ to obtain 36.0 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: The resultant force in the direction of motion of an instrumented crash-test carriage (mass 2.0 kg, initial speed 5.0 m s⁻¹) is plotted over 10.0 m. Determine its speed at x = 10.0 m.
items.workedSolution: Positive work (0 to 8 m) = ½(8 + 4)(12) = 72.0 J. Resistive work (8 m to 10 m) = −½(2)(4) = −4.00 J. Net work W = 68.0 J. From ½mv² = ½mu₀² + W, v = √(5² + 2 × 68.0 / 2) = 9.64 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds net work W = 68.0 J and v = √(5² + 2W/2) = 9.64 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Along a horizontal guideway, a low-friction dynamics trolley of mass 0.8 kg moves in a fixed direction. Its momentum–time graph shows an impulse stage from t = 1.0 s to t = 5.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resultant force F = Δp / Δt = (7.2 − 1.6) / (5 − 1) = 1.40 N. (b) Net work W = ΔE_k = (7.2² − 1.6²) / (2 × 0.8) = 30.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant force as gradient Δp / Δt of the p–t graph.
Obtains F = 1.40 N.
Relates net work to ΔE_k = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m).
Substitutes p₁ = 1.6 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ = 7.2 kg m s⁻¹, and m = 0.8 kg.
Obtains W = 30.8 J.

items.stem: Using crocodile clips with constant contact resistance R₀, a student measures total resistance R of a carbon-loaded antistatic composite bar for different length-to-area ratios (L / A) up to 500.0 m⁻¹, so R = ρ(L / A) + R₀. From the plotted line, what is the resistivity ρ of the material?
items.workedSolution: Since R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, resistivity ρ equals the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (36 − 7) / 500 = 0.0580 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 7 Ω to obtain ρ = (36 − 7) / 500 = 0.0580 Ω m (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant ratio R_max / (L/A)_max from the origin and fails to subtract the non-zero contact-resistance intercept R₀.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Adds the zero-offset intercept R₀ to R_max instead of subtracting it when finding ΔR.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Δ(L/A) / ΔR (electrical conductivity σ) instead of ΔR / Δ(L/A).

items.stem: The terminal potential difference V of a zinc-carbon dry cell decreases linearly with load current I from 0.0 A to 1.0 A, as shown. What is the mean terminal potential difference across this current range?
items.workedSolution: Terminal p.d. varies linearly from 4.5 V at I = 0.0 A to 1.5 V at I = 1 A, so V_mean = ½(4.5 + 1.5) = 3.00 V.

markScheme.criterion: Averages endpoint voltages ½(4.5 + 1.5) = 3.00 V (B).

items.stem: A capacitor in a sensor-decay demonstration discharges through a resistor R = 20 kΩ. The straight-line graph of ln(V / V) against t passes through (0 s, 1.609) and (16 s, -0.391). What is the capacitance of the capacitor?
items.workedSolution: Gradient m = (-0.391 − 1.609) / (16 − 0) = -0.1250 s⁻¹. Time constant τ = −1/m = 8.000 s. Capacitance C = τ / R = 8.000 s / (20 × 10³ Ω) = 400 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 400 μF.

items.stem: Telemetry for an underground mine haulage skip begins at t = 0.0 s when it is stationary 50.0 m beyond the shaft loading datum. Its velocity–time profile over the 15.0 s run is plotted, with braking starting at t = 9.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Trapezium area Δx = ½(15 + 6)(22) = 231 m. (b) Final distance from datum = 50 + 231 = 281 m. (c) Mean speed = 231 / 15 = 15.4 m s⁻¹. (d) Braking acceleration = (0 − 22) / (15 − 9) = -3.67 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Identifies distance travelled as the area under the v–t trapezium.
Obtains Δx = 231 m.
Adds 50 m offset to obtain 281 m.
Divides distance travelled from (a) by 15 s.
Obtains mean speed = 15.4 m s⁻¹.
Obtains braking acceleration = -3.67 m s⁻².

workingSteps: Distance equals the trapezium area under the v–t curve.

parts.prompt: Hence state its final distance from the shaft loading datum at t = 15.0 s.
Determine the mean speed over the 15.0 s run.
Calculate the acceleration between t = 9.0 s and t = 15.0 s.

items.stem: Stress–strain data for a high-density polyethylene filament are plotted up to strain 0.8, showing an initial Hookean region from 0.0 to strain 0.4 followed by reduced stiffness.
items.workedSolution: (a) Young's modulus E = 140 / 0.4 = 350 MPa. (b) Energy per unit volume = ½(0.4)(140) + ½(140 + 200)(0.4) = 96.0 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial gradient σ / ε up to ε = 0.4.
Obtains E = 350 MPa.
Identifies work per unit volume as total area under the σ–ε graph.
Splits area into initial triangle plus upper trapezium.
Obtains 96.0 MJ m⁻³.

parts.prompt: Determine the Young's modulus of the specimen over the proportional region (0.0 to 0.4).
Calculate the work done per unit volume in stretching the specimen from zero strain to 0.8.
workingSteps: Area from 0 to 0.4 = ½(0.4)(140) = 28.0 MJ m⁻³.
Area from 0.4 to 0.8 = ½(140 + 200)(0.4) = 68.0 MJ m⁻³; total = 96.0 MJ m⁻³.

items.stem: Repulsive force data between silvered glass spheres positioned above a digital load pan are transformed to F against r⁻² up to 80.0 m⁻², revealing a constant tare intercept.
items.workedSolution: (a) At r⁻² = 0, systematic tare offset F₀ = 0.200 N. (b) Gradient = (2.2 − 0.2) / 80 = 0.0250 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Reads intercept F₀ = 0.200 N.
Evaluates ΔF = 2.2 − 0.2 using intercept from (a).
Divides ΔF by 80 m⁻² and states correct unit N m².
Obtains 0.0250 N m².

items.stem: In a circuits practical, a student records the potential difference V across a tungsten filament indicator lamp as the current I is increased from 0.0 A to 1.2 A, obtaining the non-linear characteristic shown.
items.workedSolution: (a) At I = 1.2 A, V = 8.40 V. (b) Static resistance R = V / I = 8.4 / 1.2 = 7.00 Ω (the upper segment gradient 12.0 Ω is ΔV / ΔI, not R).

markScheme.criterion: Reads V = 8.40 V at I = 1.2 A.
Selects R = V / I rather than local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI.
Substitutes V = 8.4 V and I = 1.2 A.
Obtains R = 7.00 Ω.

items.stem: A student investigates a calibrated bench force spring and plots the suppressed-origin graph shown, with vertical error bars of ±0.01 m. Two widely separated coordinates on the line of best fit are (7.0 N, 0.3118 m) and (23.0 N, 0.4942 m). The steepest straight line still passing through all error bars has gradient 9.900 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) m_best = (0.4942 − 0.3118) / (23.0 − 7.0) = 0.01140 m N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0114 m N⁻¹. (b) Δm = |9.900 × 10⁻³ − 0.01140| = 1.50 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹. (c) A suppressed origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitutes large-triangle coordinates (0.4942 − 0.3118) / (23.0 − 7.0).
Obtains best-fit gradient = 0.0114 m N⁻¹ with correct compound SI unit.
Calculates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 1.50 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹.
States that a false origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

items.stem: The Cartesian plot shows experimental (V, I) data and the straight line of best fit for a uniform resistance-alloy wire of length 1.25 m and cross-sectional area 6.00 × 10⁻⁸ m². The line of best fit passes through the origin and reaches I = 0.500 A at V = 6.00 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) Gradient = 0.08333 A V⁻¹, so R = 1 / gradient = 12.0 Ω. (c) ρ = RA/L = 5.760 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 5.76 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.
Correctly specifies all quantities (or notes constant temperature / material property).
Computes large-triangle gradient m = ΔI/ΔV = 0.0833 A V⁻¹ and takes its reciprocal R = 1/m.
Correct wire resistance R = 12.0 Ω.
Substitutes R, A, and L correctly into ρ = RA/L.
Correct resistivity 5.76 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m with unit Ω m.

parts.expectedAnswer: Electrical resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area, where resistance, cross-sectional area, and length are measured for a uniform specimen at constant temperature.

items.stem: On a horizontal frictionless bench, a linear valve return spring is compressed by 0.4 m according to the force–compression graph shown and released from rest to propel a 0.22 kg block. What launch speed does the block acquire?
items.workedSolution: Elastic energy stored E_p = ½(44)(0.4) = 8.80 J. Equating ½mv² = E_p gives v = √(2 × 8.80 / 0.22) = 8.94 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Sets ½(0.22)v² = 8.80 J to obtain v = 8.94 m s⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: The graph displays how the velocity of a robotic warehouse retrieval carriage along a straight aisle rail varies with time over 12.0 s. Positive velocity corresponds to motion forward, and direction reversal occurs during the linear ramp between t = 6.0 s and t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero-velocity crossing is at t = 9 s. Positive area = 54.0 m and unsigned negative area = 7.50 m, giving total distance = 61.5 m. (b) Net displacement = 54.0 − 7.50 = 46.5 m; average velocity = 46.5 / 12 = 3.88 m s⁻¹. (c) Acceleration = (−3 − 9) / (10 − 6) = -3.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Finds zero-crossing t = 9 s and evaluates both unsigned areas (54.0 m and 7.50 m).
Obtains total distance = 61.5 m.
Subtracts areas for net displacement (46.5 m) and divides by 12 s.
Obtains average velocity = 3.88 m s⁻¹.
Obtains acceleration = -3.00 m s⁻² including negative sign.

parts.prompt: Calculate the total distance travelled between t = 0.0 s and t = 12.0 s.
workingSteps: Velocity crosses zero at t = 9 s; forward area = 54.0 m.
Unsigned reverse area = 7.50 m, so total distance = 54.0 + 7.50 = 61.5 m.

parts.prompt: Determine the net displacement and hence calculate the average velocity over the 12.0 s interval.
workingSteps: Average velocity = Δs / Δt = 46.5 / 12 = 3.88 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the acceleration between t = 6.0 s and t = 10.0 s.

items.stem: A force transducer logs a 2.5 s solenoid kicker stroke acting forward on a robotic soccer puck (mass 3.0 kg), which had momentum 9.0 kg m s⁻¹ at t = 0.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Impulse J = ½(2.5 + 1.5)(46) = 92.0 N s. (b) Final momentum p_f = 9 + 92.0 = 101 kg m s⁻¹. (c) Speed increase Δv = 92.0 / 3 = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes impulse from the trapezium area under the F–t curve.
Obtains J = 92.0 N s.
Adds 9 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 101 kg m s⁻¹.
Divides impulse from (a) by 3 kg.
Obtains Δv = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The I–V characteristic graph shown (current I on the vertical axis against potential difference V on the horizontal axis) was recorded for a constantan wire coil. Which physical explanation correctly describes the shape of this characteristic?
items.workedSolution: On an I–V graph (I on the vertical axis, V on the horizontal axis), gradient equals reciprocal of resistance. For this ohmic metallic resistor at constant temperature, constant resistance because current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly identifies that constant resistance because current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature.

options.label: A
options.text: Resistance increases smoothly with voltage because the gradient of the straight line is constant.
options.distractorRationale: Constant gradient on an I–V graph means constant resistance, not increasing resistance.

options.label: B
options.text: It exhibits constant resistance because current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature.

options.label: C
options.text: Resistance equals the gradient of the I–V line rather than its reciprocal.
options.distractorRationale: With I on the vertical axis and V on the horizontal axis, gradient equals 1/R.

options.label: D
options.text: Current flows only above a forward threshold potential difference.

items.stem: The straight-line charging graph for a timing-circuit capacitor extends from (0, 0) to a final state of Q = 3.60 mC and V = 8.00 V. Using the area under the graph, what is the electrical energy stored in the capacitor?
items.workedSolution: Triangular area under the linear graph gives E = ½ Q V = 0.5 × (3.6 × 10⁻³ C) × 8 V = 0.01440 J ≈ 0.0144 J.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly converts mC to C and obtains 0.0144 J.

items.stem: The signed upward acceleration of a deep-sea winch capsule is plotted from t = 0.0 s to t = 15.0 s; at the start of the recording, its velocity is 15.0 m s⁻¹ upward.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum speed occurs when acceleration crosses zero from positive to negative at t = 8.00 s. (b) Positive area = 52.0 m s⁻¹, giving v_max = 15 + 52.0 = 67.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Negative area magnitude = 24.0 m s⁻¹, so v_final = 67.0 − 24.0 = 43.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: States t = 8.00 s.
Evaluates positive area up to 8 s (52.0 m s⁻¹) and adds u₀ = 15 m s⁻¹.
Obtains v_max = 67.0 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts negative area (24.0 m s⁻¹) from v_max.
Obtains final velocity = 43.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Force-transducer and encoder data for a linear dynamo test sled (mass 1.6 kg, speed 4.5 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.0 m) are plotted over a 8.0 m straight track.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates positive (54.0 J) and negative (−4.00 J) areas.
Obtains net work W = 50.0 J.
Uses ½mv² = ½(1.6)(4.5²) + W.
Obtains v = 9.10 m s⁻¹.
Divides net work by 8 m to get 6.25 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net work done on the 1.6 kg object between x = 0.0 m and x = 8.0 m.
workingSteps: Positive area (0 to 6 m) = ½(6 + 3)(12) = 54.0 J; negative area (6 m to 8 m) = −½(2)(4) = −4.00 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate its speed at x = 8.0 m.
State the mean resultant force over the 8.0 m displacement.

items.stem: In a linear dynamics experiment, a superconducting levitation carrier of mass 2.4 kg moves in a straight line with momentum varying as shown. How much net work is done on it between t = 3.0 s and t = 7.0 s?
items.workedSolution: Using E_k = p² / (2m), net work W = ΔE_k = (16.8² − 4.8²) / (2 × 2.4) = 54.0 J.

items.stem: Two-terminal ohmmeter data R for a sintered silicon-carbide heating rod of varying dimensions are graphed versus L / A from 0.0 m⁻¹ to 50.0 m⁻¹ as shown below.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical intercept R₀ = 4.00 Ω. (b) Resistivity ρ = (20 − 4) / 50 = 0.320 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States R₀ = 4.00 Ω.
Identifies ρ with the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).
Subtracts R₀ = 4 Ω from 20 Ω before dividing by 50 m⁻¹.
Obtains ρ = 0.320 Ω m.

items.stem: Calibrated meters measure terminal potential difference V versus current I up to 5.0 A for a rechargeable nickel-cadmium pack, as plotted on the axes.
items.workedSolution: (a) Open-circuit intercept gives ε = 25.0 V. (b) Gradient = (10 − 25) / 5 = -3.00 V A⁻¹. (c) Mean terminal p.d. = ½(25 + 10) = 17.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reads ε = 25.0 V at I = 0.
Evaluates (10 − 25) / 5 including negative sign.
Obtains -3.00 V A⁻¹.
Uses ½(25 + 10) or area divided by 5 A.
Obtains 17.5 V.

items.stem: In the rigid nitrogen gas thermometer investigation, each scale position on a metre rule is read with an absolute uncertainty of ±1.0 mm. When calculating extension e = L₂ − L₁ from two separate scale readings, what is the absolute uncertainty Δe?
items.workedSolution: When subtracting two measurements, absolute uncertainties add: Δe = ΔL₁ + ΔL₂ = 1.0 + 1.0 = 2.00 mm (whereas percentage uncertainty in the graph gradient is 16.3%).

markScheme.criterion: Adds absolute uncertainties of both scale readings to obtain 2.00 mm.

items.stem: A charged capacitor in a precision capacitance tester discharges through a fixed 40 kΩ resistor. The linear plot of ln(V / V) against time t passes through the vertical intercept (0 s, 2.485) and the endpoint (48 s, 0.485).
items.workedSolution: (a) taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference. (b) Gradient m = -0.04167 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/m = 24.00 s ≈ 24.0 s. (c) C = τ/R = 600 μF. (d) uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

markScheme.criterion: Shows taking natural logs produces a linear relation between ln(V) and t.
Identifies gradient = −1/τ and vertical intercept = ln(V₀).
Evaluates negative gradient m = -0.0417 s⁻¹ and uses τ = −1/m.
Correct time constant τ = 24.0 s.
Correct capacitance C = τ / R = 600 μF.
States that it uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

parts.prompt: Explain why plotting the natural logarithm of potential difference against time yields a straight line, identifying the physical meaning of its gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: From the exponential discharge equation, taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference.
workingSteps: Take natural logarithms of both sides of the exponential decay equation.
Compare with a linear equation to identify the negative gradient and the vertical intercept.

parts.prompt: Determine the time constant τ of the RC circuit from the gradient of the graph.
workingSteps: Time constant τ = −1 / m = 24.00 s ≈ 24.0 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in μF given R = 40 kΩ.
State why determining τ from the gradient of a ln(V) against t graph is more reliable than drawing an initial tangent to a V against t curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The logarithmic gradient method is more reliable because it uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.
workingSteps: Drawing a tangent to a curve by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise at a single point, whereas a linear best-fit averages random errors over all readings.

items.stem: In the velocity–time record for a linear-induction baggage carrier (initially 30.0 m from the sorting-hall origin sensor), uniform braking begins at t = 8.0 s and ends at rest at t = 12.0 s. Find the signed braking acceleration.
items.workedSolution: During braking from t = 8 s to t = 12 s, a = (0 − 14) / (12 − 8) = -3.50 m s⁻².

items.stem: In a tensile materials test, an extruded fluoropolymer ribbon obeys Hooke's law up to a strain of 0.2 before softening up to strain 0.4, as shown on the stress–strain graph. What is the Young's modulus of the material in the initial linear region?
items.workedSolution: Up to the limit of proportionality at ε = 0.2, stress reaches 150 MPa. Young's modulus E = σ / ε = 150 / 0.2 = 750 MPa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial linear gradient E = 150 / 0.2 = 750 MPa (D).

items.stem: To test Coulomb's inverse-square law using charged metallized spheres in a Coulomb torsion-balance rig with an unzeroed tare offset F₀, the force reading F is plotted against inverse-square separation (r⁻²) up to 100.0 m⁻², following F = k|Q₁Q₂|r⁻² + F₀. What is the gradient k|Q₁Q₂| of the line?
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.2 N; at r⁻² = 100 m⁻², F = 1.8 N. Gradient = (1.8 − 0.2) / 100 = 0.0160 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.2 N to get (1.8 − 0.2) / 100 = 0.0160 N m² (B).

options.label: D

items.stem: Using the plotted V–I characteristic of a miniature krypton torch lamp, calculate its static resistance R at an operating current of 2.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 2 A, V = 16.5 V, so R = 16.5 / 2 = 8.25 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 16.5 / 2 = 8.25 Ω (C).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Evaluates the low-current resistance near the origin rather than at the specified operating current.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Calculates the local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI instead of the static ratio V / I defining electrical resistance.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Inverts the ratio to I / V (conductance in S) rather than V / I.

items.stem: During uncertainty analysis of a capillary Poiseuille flow experiment, the shallowest worst-fit line is constructed across the domain 4.0 kPa to 20.0 kPa. Determine the gradient of the plotted line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 4 kPa, y₁ = 12 mL s⁻¹; at x₂ = 20 kPa, y₂ = 56 mL s⁻¹. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (56 − 12) / (20 − 4) = 2.75 mL s⁻¹ kPa⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (56 − 12) / (20 − 4) = 2.75 mL s⁻¹ kPa⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: When finding the best-fit gradient from the false-origin graph of the heavy-duty steel workshop spring, the dashed triangle spans more than half the plotted range. Why is a large gradient triangle essential?
items.workedSolution: On a suppressed-origin NCUK graph, the procedure reduces percentage reading uncertainty when calculating the gradient.

markScheme.criterion: States accurately that the graphing technique reduces percentage reading uncertainty when calculating the gradient.

options.text: Because it reduces percentage reading uncertainty when calculating the gradient

options.label: C
options.text: It removes random scatter from the plotted experimental crosses completely
options.distractorRationale: Random scatter is already fixed in the recorded data points.

options.label: D
options.text: It allows the student to pick two raw plotted data crosses instead of points on the best-fit line
options.distractorRationale: Gradient triangles should always use widely separated points lying directly on the line of best fit.

items.stem: Speed-squared readings v² are graphed against displacement s (0.0 m to 2.0 m) for a steel ball bearing rolling in a V-channel with negligible rotational loss on a frictionless ramp of sin θ = 0.2 where g = 9.81 m s⁻². Calculate the gradient of the line.
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 2.2 m² s⁻² and at s = 2 m, v² = 10.048 m² s⁻². Gradient = (10.048 − 2.2) / 2 = 2(9.81)(0.2) = 3.92 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 2.2 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.81 × 0.2) to get 3.92 m s⁻² (D).

items.workedSolution: From t = 8 s to t = 16 s, displacement changes from 46 m to 22 m. Velocity v = (22 − 46) / (16 − 8) = -3.00 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A student plots current I (y-axis) against potential difference V (x-axis) for a uniform constantan wire of length 1.60 m and cross-sectional area 8.00 × 10⁻⁸ m². The straight line of best fit passes through the origin and the point (8.00 V, 0.800 A). What is the resistivity of the constantan?
items.workedSolution: Gradient m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.8000 A / 8.000 V = 0.1000 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 10.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 5.000 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 5.00 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: Calibration measurements up to 0.8 m for an optical-mount preload spring are graphed below; at full compression it propels a stationary 0.6 kg slider along a level frictionless rail.
items.workedSolution: (a) k = 92 / 0.8 = 115 N m⁻¹. (b) Elastic energy E_p = ½(92)(0.8) = 36.8 J. (c) Launch speed v = √(2(36.8)/0.6) = 11.1 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies k as the gradient ΔF / Δx.
Obtains k = 115 N m⁻¹.
Uses triangular area ½Fx.
Obtains E_p = 36.8 J.
Equates ½(0.6)v² to stored elastic energy from (b).

options.label: A
options.distractorRationale: Assumes ln C drops to zero at t = t_max instead of subtracting the non-zero final ordinate ln C(t_max).

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Computes λ = |Δ(ln C) / Δt| correctly in magnitude but omits the negative sign of the downward semi-log slope.

options.label: C
options.distractorRationale: Inverts Δt / Δ(ln C) to obtain −1/λ (negative mean lifetime) instead of the gradient −λ.

items.stem: Telemetry from a cable-hauled alpine service car operating on a straight haulage section is plotted on the velocity–time axes shown (uphill positive). What total path distance is covered over the 10.0 s run?
items.workedSolution: Velocity crosses zero at t = 7 s. Forward area (0 to 7 s) = ½(2)(6) + (2)(6) + ½(3)(6) = 27.0 m. Reverse area magnitude (7 s to 10 s) = ½(1)(2) + (2)(2) = 5.00 m. Total distance = 27.0 + 5.00 = 32.0 m.

markScheme.criterion: Sums unsigned positive (27.0 m) and negative (5.00 m) velocity–time areas to obtain 32.0 m (A).

items.stem: Moving in a straight line with initial momentum 4.5 kg m s⁻¹, a ballistic pendulum carriage (mass 1.5 kg) undergoes the 1.6 s controlled gas-jet pulse shown. What is its final momentum at t = 1.6 s?
items.workedSolution: Impulse Δp = ½(1.6 + 0.8)(40) = 48.0 N s. Final momentum p_f = p₀ + Δp = 4.5 + 48.0 = 52.5 kg m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Adds impulse (48.0 N s) to p₀ = 4.5 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 52.5 kg m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: The graph shows the I–V characteristic recorded for a bead NTC thermistor in an NCUK laboratory investigation, with current plotted on the vertical axis and potential difference on the horizontal axis. At the highlighted operating point, V = 8.00 V and I = 0.800 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = V / I = 10.00 Ω ≈ 10.0 Ω. (b) connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the component and reverse the supply connections for negative readings. (c) resistance decreases as temperature increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.

Correct static resistance 10.0 Ω.
Specifies potential divider (or variable supply) with series ammeter and parallel voltmeter.
Includes a series protective resistor and reversing supply connections for negative voltages.
Correctly describes how resistance changes across the graph.
Correct microscopic explanation: resistance decreases as temperature increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.

workingSteps: Recall that static resistance at a point is R = V / I (not the inverse of the local tangent).
Substitute V = 8.000 V and I = 0.8000 A to obtain R = 10.00 Ω ≈ 10.0 Ω.

parts.prompt: Describe the circuit arrangement and experimental procedure used to obtain a complete I–V characteristic safely across positive and negative potential differences.
parts.expectedAnswer: To obtain the full characteristic safely, connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the component and reverse the supply connections for negative readings.
workingSteps: Use a potential divider to vary potential difference smoothly from zero while limiting excessive current with a protective resistor.
Measure current with a series ammeter, potential difference with a parallel voltmeter, and reverse the supply leads for negative polarity.

parts.prompt: Explain the physical shape of the I–V characteristic in terms of charge carriers and resistance.
parts.expectedAnswer: The curve shows that the component resistance decreases as temperature increases because more charge carriers are released so the curve becomes steeper.
workingSteps: Link the changing ratio of potential difference to current directly to the microscopic conduction mechanism.

items.stem: The graph shows how charge Q and potential difference V vary as a dc-bus decoupling capacitor is charged uniformly from zero up to Q = 7.50 mC at V = 15.0 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates. (b) C = Q / V = 500 μF. (c) Triangular area E = ½ Q V = 0.05625 J ≈ 0.0562 J.

markScheme.criterion: States charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
Correct capacitance 500 μF.
Recognises triangular area E = ½ Q V and converts mC to C.
Correct stored energy 0.0562 J.

parts.expectedAnswer: Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
workingSteps: State the definition as the ratio of charge stored to potential difference.

parts.prompt: Deduce the capacitance of the capacitor from the graph in μF.
Determine the electrical energy stored in the capacitor using the shaded triangular area under the graph.
workingSteps: Because V increases linearly from 0 to V_max as charge builds up, energy stored equals the triangular area E = ½ Q V.

items.stem: Over an interval of 10.0 s, a maglev propulsion test pod (initial velocity 8.0 m s⁻¹ eastward) follows the plotted acceleration profile. What velocity does it have when t = 10.0 s?
items.workedSolution: Positive a–t area (0 to 5 s) = 28.0 m s⁻¹; negative area magnitude (5 s to 10 s) = 16.0 m s⁻¹. Net Δv = 28.0 − 16.0 = 12.0 m s⁻¹. Final velocity = 8 + (12.0) = 20.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines net signed area (12.0 m s⁻¹) with u₀ = 8 m s⁻¹ to obtain 20.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Passing x = 0.0 m with speed 4.0 m s⁻¹, a magnetic-launch coaster bogie of mass 3.2 kg experiences the collinear resultant force plotted against displacement up to x = 14.0 m. What is its speed at x = 14.0 m?
items.workedSolution: Positive work (0 to 11 m) = ½(11 + 6)(16) = 136 J. Resistive work (11 m to 14 m) = −½(3)(4) = −6.00 J. Net work W = 130 J. From ½mv² = ½mu₀² + W, v = √(4² + 2 × 130 / 3.2) = 9.86 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Finds net work W = 130 J and v = √(4² + 2W/3.2) = 9.86 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: Along a horizontal guideway, a satellite attitude-test mass of mass 0.8 kg moves in a fixed direction. Its momentum–time graph shows an impulse stage from t = 1.0 s to t = 5.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resultant force F = Δp / Δt = (7.2 − 1.6) / (5 − 1) = 1.40 N. (b) Net work W = ΔE_k = (7.2² − 1.6²) / (2 × 0.8) = 30.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant force as gradient Δp / Δt of the p–t graph.
Obtains F = 1.40 N.
Relates net work to ΔE_k = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m).
Substitutes p₁ = 1.6 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ = 7.2 kg m s⁻¹, and m = 0.8 kg.
Obtains W = 30.8 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resultant force acting between t = 1.0 s and t = 5.0 s.
Calculate the net work done on the 0.8 kg object between t = 1.0 s and t = 5.0 s.
workingSteps: Use E_k = p² / (2m) before and after the force acts.

items.stem: In a materials conductivity test on a sintered silicon-carbide heating rod, measured resistance R varies linearly with L / A up to 80.0 m⁻¹ as shown. Extract the bulk resistivity ρ.
items.workedSolution: Since R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, resistivity ρ equals the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (25 − 5) / 80 = 0.250 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 5 Ω to obtain ρ = (25 − 5) / 80 = 0.250 Ω m (A).

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant ratio R_max / (L/A)_max from the origin and fails to subtract the non-zero contact-resistance intercept R₀.

items.stem: A variable load resistor is connected across a nickel-metal-hydride battery pack, and the terminal potential difference V is plotted against current I up to 2.0 A. According to V = ε − Ir, what is the signed gradient of this graph?
items.workedSolution: At I = 0.0 A, V = ε = 7 V; at I = 2 A, V = 3.4 V. Gradient = (3.4 − 7) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (equal to −r).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates (3.4 − 7) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (A).

options.distractorRationale: Assumes the line meets V = 0 at I = I_max instead of reading the non-zero terminal voltage V(I_max).

items.stem: A capacitor in a student data-logger RC circuit discharges through a resistor R = 40 kΩ. The straight-line graph of ln(V / V) against t passes through (0 s, 2.303) and (40 s, 0.303). What is the capacitance of the capacitor?
items.workedSolution: Gradient m = (0.303 − 2.303) / (40 − 0) = -0.05000 s⁻¹. Time constant τ = −1/m = 20.00 s. Capacitance C = τ / R = 20.00 s / (40 × 10³ Ω) = 500 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 500 μF.

items.stem: Telemetry for a solar-powered desert research rover begins at t = 0.0 s when it is stationary 50.0 m beyond the base-camp beacon. Its velocity–time profile over the 15.0 s run is plotted, with braking starting at t = 9.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Trapezium area Δx = ½(15 + 6)(22) = 231 m. (b) Final distance from datum = 50 + 231 = 281 m. (c) Mean speed = 231 / 15 = 15.4 m s⁻¹. (d) Braking acceleration = (0 − 22) / (15 − 9) = -3.67 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Identifies distance travelled as the area under the v–t trapezium.
Obtains Δx = 231 m.
Adds 50 m offset to obtain 281 m.
Divides distance travelled from (a) by 15 s.
Obtains mean speed = 15.4 m s⁻¹.

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance travelled during the 15.0 s journey.
workingSteps: Distance equals the trapezium area under the v–t curve.

parts.prompt: Hence state its final distance from the base-camp beacon at t = 15.0 s.
Determine the mean speed over the 15.0 s run.
Calculate the acceleration between t = 9.0 s and t = 15.0 s.

items.stem: The plotted tensile stress–strain profile for a thermoplastic elastomer tether exhibits a distinct gradient change at the limit of proportionality (strain 0.4) before reaching strain 0.8.
items.workedSolution: (a) Young's modulus E = 170 / 0.4 = 425 MPa. (b) Energy per unit volume = ½(0.4)(170) + ½(170 + 240)(0.4) = 116 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial gradient σ / ε up to ε = 0.4.
Obtains E = 425 MPa.
Identifies work per unit volume as total area under the σ–ε graph.
Splits area into initial triangle plus upper trapezium.
Obtains 116 MJ m⁻³.

parts.prompt: Determine the Young's modulus of the specimen over the proportional region (0.0 to 0.4).
Calculate the work done per unit volume in stretching the specimen from zero strain to 0.8.
workingSteps: Area from 0 to 0.4 = ½(0.4)(170) = 34.0 MJ m⁻³.
Area from 0.4 to 0.8 = ½(170 + 240)(0.4) = 82.0 MJ m⁻³; total = 116 MJ m⁻³.

items.stem: Refer to the linearized Coulomb graph of balance reading F against r⁻² (up to 80.0 m⁻²) recorded using precision electrostatic spheres on a sapphire-pivot balance.
items.workedSolution: (a) At r⁻² = 0, systematic tare offset F₀ = 0.400 N. (b) Gradient = (2.4 − 0.4) / 80 = 0.0250 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Reads intercept F₀ = 0.400 N.
Evaluates ΔF = 2.4 − 0.4 using intercept from (a).
Divides ΔF by 80 m⁻² and states correct unit N m².
Obtains 0.0250 N m².

items.workedSolution: (a) At I = 1.2 A, V = 8.40 V. (b) Static resistance R = V / I = 8.4 / 1.2 = 7.00 Ω (the upper segment gradient 9.50 Ω is ΔV / ΔI, not R).

items.stem: A student investigates a heavy-duty steel workshop spring and plots the suppressed-origin graph shown, with vertical error bars of ±0.014 m. Two widely separated coordinates on the line of best fit are (9.0 N, 0.4802 m) and (27.0 N, 0.7106 m). The steepest straight line still passing through all error bars has gradient 0.01105 m N⁻¹. The specimen diameter is measured as d = 0.92 ± 0.024 mm.
items.workedSolution: (a) m_best = (0.7106 − 0.4802) / (27.0 − 9.0) = 0.01280 m N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0128 m N⁻¹. (b) Δm = |0.01105 − 0.01280| = 1.75 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹. (c) A suppressed origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision. (d) %Δm = 13.67%, %ΔA = 2 × %Δd = 5.217%, total = 18.89% ≈ 18.9%.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitutes large-triangle coordinates (0.7106 − 0.4802) / (27.0 − 9.0).
Obtains best-fit gradient = 0.0128 m N⁻¹ with correct compound SI unit.
Calculates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 1.75 × 10⁻³ m N⁻¹.
States that a false origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.
Evaluates %Δm = 13.7% and %ΔA = 2 × %Δd = 5.22%.
Sums percentage uncertainties to obtain 18.9%.

items.stem: The Cartesian plot shows experimental (V, I) data and the straight line of best fit for a uniform german-silver alloy of length 1.60 m and cross-sectional area 6.40 × 10⁻⁸ m². The line of best fit passes through the origin and reaches I = 1.00 A at V = 8.00 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) Gradient = 0.1250 A V⁻¹, so R = 1 / gradient = 8.00 Ω. (c) ρ = RA/L = 3.200 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 3.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

parts.prompt: Define the electrical resistivity of a material.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrical resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area, where resistance, cross-sectional area, and length are measured for a uniform specimen at constant temperature.
workingSteps: State the definition in terms of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area.
Identify that resistivity is an intrinsic property of the material at constant temperature.

parts.prompt: Determine the resistance of the wire from the gradient of the I–V line of best fit using a large triangle.
workingSteps: Because I is on the vertical axis, R = 1 / m = 8.000 Ω ≈ 8.00 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the alloy, stating the appropriate SI unit.
workingSteps: Evaluate ρ = 3.200 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 3.20 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: Inspect the straight-line applied force versus extension plot (up to 0.5 m) for a laboratory catapult tension spring. Evaluate the spring constant k.
items.workedSolution: Spring constant k = gradient ΔF / Δx = 30 / 0.5 = 60.0 N m⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates gradient k = 30 / 0.5 = 60.0 N m⁻¹ (D).

items.stem: A laboratory team investigates exponential decay in a positron-emitting fluorine tracer vial using a coincidence ring detector, obtaining the straight-line graph of ln(C / s⁻¹) against t up to 80.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical intercept at t = 0 is ln(C₀ / s⁻¹) = 8.80. (b) Gradient = (2.4 − 8.8) / 80 = -0.0800 s⁻¹ (which equals −λ).

items.stem: In a laboratory motion trial, a robotic warehouse retrieval carriage travels along a straight aisle rail with forward taken as positive. The velocity–time graph records its motion from t = 0.0 s to t = 12.0 s, including uniform reversal thrust from t = 6.0 s to t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero-velocity crossing is at t = 9 s. Positive area = 108 m and unsigned negative area = 15.0 m, giving total distance = 123 m. (b) Net displacement = 108 − 15.0 = 93.0 m; average velocity = 93.0 / 12 = 7.75 m s⁻¹. (c) Acceleration = (−6 − 18) / (10 − 6) = -6.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Finds zero-crossing t = 9 s and evaluates both unsigned areas (108 m and 15.0 m).
Obtains total distance = 123 m.
Subtracts areas for net displacement (93.0 m) and divides by 12 s.
Obtains average velocity = 7.75 m s⁻¹.
Obtains acceleration = -6.00 m s⁻² including negative sign.

items.stem: A force transducer logs a 2.5 s cold-gas thruster burn acting forward on a cold-gas attitude probe (mass 3.0 kg), which had momentum 9.0 kg m s⁻¹ at t = 0.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Impulse J = ½(2.5 + 1.5)(46) = 92.0 N s. (b) Final momentum p_f = 9 + 92.0 = 101 kg m s⁻¹. (c) Speed increase Δv = 92.0 / 3 = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes impulse from the trapezium area under the F–t curve.
Obtains J = 92.0 N s.
Adds 9 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 101 kg m s⁻¹.
Divides impulse from (a) by 3 kg.
Obtains Δv = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The I–V characteristic graph for a daylight-sensor strip highlights an operating point where V = 4.00 V and I = 0.400 A. What is the static resistance of the component at this operating point?
items.workedSolution: Static resistance at any point on an I–V graph is R = V / I = 4.000 V / 0.4000 A = 10.00 Ω ≈ 10.0 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates R = V / I accurately to obtain 10.0 Ω.

items.stem: The charging graph for a bench super-film capacitor is a straight line from the origin to Q = 8.00 mC at V = 20.0 V. What is the capacitance of the capacitor?
items.workedSolution: Convert Q = 8 mC = 8.000 × 10⁻³ C. Capacitance C = Q / V = 4.000 × 10⁻⁴ F = 400 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly converts mC to C and obtains 400 μF.

items.stem: An inertial sensor logs the acceleration of a linear-motor brake-test bogie over a 20.0 s interval (along the track positive). At t = 0.0 s its velocity is 17.0 m s⁻¹ along the track.
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum speed occurs when acceleration crosses zero from positive to negative at t = 10.0 s. (b) Positive area = 48.0 m s⁻¹, giving v_max = 17 + 48.0 = 65.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Negative area magnitude = 15.0 m s⁻¹, so v_final = 65.0 − 15.0 = 50.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: States t = 10.0 s.
Evaluates positive area up to 10 s (48.0 m s⁻¹) and adds u₀ = 17 m s⁻¹.
Obtains v_max = 65.0 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts negative area (15.0 m s⁻¹) from v_max.
Obtains final velocity = 50.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Force-transducer and encoder data for an instrumented crash-test carriage (mass 1.6 kg, speed 4.5 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.0 m) are plotted over a 8.0 m straight track.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates positive (54.0 J) and negative (−4.00 J) areas.
Obtains net work W = 50.0 J.
Uses ½mv² = ½(1.6)(4.5²) + W.
Obtains v = 9.10 m s⁻¹.
Divides net work by 8 m to get 6.25 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net work done on the 1.6 kg object between x = 0.0 m and x = 8.0 m.
workingSteps: Positive area (0 to 6 m) = ½(6 + 3)(12) = 54.0 J; negative area (6 m to 8 m) = −½(2)(4) = −4.00 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate its speed at x = 8.0 m.
State the mean resultant force over the 8.0 m displacement.

items.stem: The momentum–time graph is recorded for an ice-rink calibration sled (mass 4.0 kg) travelling along a straight guide. Calculate the net work done on the object from t = 4.0 s to t = 8.0 s.
items.workedSolution: Using E_k = p² / (2m), net work W = ΔE_k = (28² − 8²) / (2 × 4) = 90.0 J.

markScheme.criterion: Applies W = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m) = (28² − 8²) / (8) = 90.0 J (C).

items.stem: The linear graph below displays total measured resistance R against L / A (0.0 m⁻¹ to 400.0 m⁻¹) during a resistivity test on a concentrated saline conductivity column.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical intercept R₀ = 10.0 Ω. (b) Resistivity ρ = (46 − 10) / 400 = 0.0900 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States R₀ = 10.0 Ω.
Identifies ρ with the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).
Subtracts R₀ = 10 Ω from 46 Ω before dividing by 400 m⁻¹.
Obtains ρ = 0.0900 Ω m.

items.stem: The straight-line plot below shows how the terminal potential difference of an alkaline lantern battery falls as load current increases from 0.0 A to 5.0 A.
items.workedSolution: (a) Open-circuit intercept gives ε = 16.0 V. (b) Gradient = (7 − 16) / 5 = -1.80 V A⁻¹. (c) Mean terminal p.d. = ½(16 + 7) = 11.5 V.

markScheme.criterion: Reads ε = 16.0 V at I = 0.
Evaluates (7 − 16) / 5 including negative sign.
Obtains -1.80 V A⁻¹.
Uses ½(16 + 7) or area divided by 5 A.
Obtains 11.5 V.

items.stem: A charged capacitor in an automatic shutter timer discharges through a fixed 50 kΩ resistor. The linear plot of ln(V / V) against time t passes through the vertical intercept (0 s, 2.303) and the endpoint (40 s, 0.303).
items.workedSolution: (a) taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference. (b) Gradient m = -0.05000 s⁻¹, so τ = −1/m = 20.00 s ≈ 20.0 s. (c) C = τ/R = 400 μF. (d) uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

markScheme.criterion: Shows taking natural logs produces a linear relation between ln(V) and t.
Identifies gradient = −1/τ and vertical intercept = ln(V₀).
Evaluates negative gradient m = -0.0500 s⁻¹ and uses τ = −1/m.
Correct time constant τ = 20.0 s.
Correct capacitance C = τ / R = 400 μF.
States that it uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.

parts.prompt: Explain why plotting the natural logarithm of potential difference against time yields a straight line, identifying the physical meaning of its gradient and vertical intercept.
parts.expectedAnswer: From the exponential discharge equation, taking natural logarithms gives a straight line with negative gradient equal to minus the reciprocal of the time constant and vertical intercept equal to the natural logarithm of the initial potential difference.
workingSteps: Take natural logarithms of both sides of the exponential decay equation.
Compare with a linear equation to identify the negative gradient and the vertical intercept.

parts.prompt: Determine the time constant τ of the RC circuit from the gradient of the graph.
workingSteps: Time constant τ = −1 / m = 20.00 s ≈ 20.0 s.

parts.prompt: Calculate the capacitance of the capacitor in μF given R = 50 kΩ.
State why determining τ from the gradient of a ln(V) against t graph is more reliable than drawing an initial tangent to a V against t curve.
parts.expectedAnswer: The logarithmic gradient method is more reliable because it uses all measured data points along a straight best fit line rather than estimating a single tangent by eye.
workingSteps: Drawing a tangent to a curve by eye is subjective and sensitive to noise at a single point, whereas a linear best-fit averages random errors over all readings.

items.stem: Over a 20.0 s transfer starting at x = 30.0 m from the western end-stop, a shipyard gantry crane crab has the velocity–time graph shown. Calculate its average speed over the 20.0 s interval.
items.workedSolution: Distance travelled Δx = ½(20 + 10)(14) = 210 m (independent of the 30 m starting offset). Mean speed = 210 / 20 = 10.5 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Divides trapezium distance (210 m) by 20 s to obtain 10.5 m s⁻¹ (B).

items.stem: The tensile stress–strain curve for a thermoplastic elastomer tether is linear from 0.0 to strain 0.3 and reaches strain 0.6. Determine the Young's modulus in MPa.
items.workedSolution: Up to the limit of proportionality at ε = 0.3, stress reaches 210 MPa. Young's modulus E = σ / ε = 210 / 0.3 = 700 MPa.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial linear gradient E = 210 / 0.3 = 700 MPa (D).

items.stem: The linearized Coulomb plot shows balance force F versus inverse-square separation r⁻² up to 80.0 m⁻² for two conducting pith spheres on a digital top-pan balance. Calculate the gradient of the line in N m².
items.workedSolution: At r⁻² = 0.0 m⁻², tare offset F₀ = 0.2 N; at r⁻² = 80 m⁻², F = 1.8 N. Gradient = (1.8 − 0.2) / 80 = 0.0200 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts tare offset F₀ = 0.2 N to get (1.8 − 0.2) / 80 = 0.0200 N m² (A).

items.stem: A student measures the V–I curve shown for a miniature incandescent beacon lamp. Determine the resistance of the device at I = 2.0 A.
items.workedSolution: Electrical resistance at an operating point is defined by R = V / I (not the local slope ΔV / ΔI). At I = 2 A, V = 15 V, so R = 15 / 2 = 7.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Uses static ratio R = V / I = 15 / 2 = 7.50 Ω (D).

items.stem: Error-bar bounds at 0.4 mW and 2.0 mW define the steepest acceptable line in an optical photodiode irradiance calibration. Evaluate the slope of this worst-fit line.
items.workedSolution: At x₁ = 0.4 mW, y₁ = 1 μA; at x₂ = 2 mW, y₂ = 6.6 μA. Worst-fit gradient m_worst = (6.6 − 1) / (2 − 0.4) = 3.50 μA mW⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δy / Δx = (6.6 − 1) / (2 − 0.4) = 3.50 μA mW⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: The suppressed-origin graph shows measurements for a steel helical suspension spring. Two widely separated read-off points on the line of best fit have coordinates (3.0 N, 0.2585 m) and (11.0 N, 0.4065 m). What is the best-fit gradient of the graph?
items.workedSolution: Using the large triangle spanning more than half the grid: gradient = (0.4065 − 0.2585) / (11.0 − 3.0) = 0.01850 m N⁻¹ ≈ 0.0185 m N⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Calculates best-fit gradient = 0.0185 m N⁻¹ from Δy / Δx.

items.stem: Using two light gates in a gravitational field g = 9.8 m s⁻², a student records speed v of a wheeled telemetry trolley accelerating along a tilted track (inclination sin θ = 0.3) after passing an initial gate at s = 0.0 m with speed u₀ > 0, plotting v² against distance s up to 2.0 m. According to v² = u₀² + 2as, what is the gradient Δ(v²) / Δs of the line?
items.workedSolution: From v² = u₀² + (2g sin θ)s, the vertical intercept is u₀² = 2.5 m² s⁻² and at s = 2 m, v² = 14.26 m² s⁻². Gradient = (14.26 − 2.5) / 2 = 2(9.8)(0.3) = 5.88 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept u₀² = 2.5 m² s⁻² (or evaluates 2 × 9.8 × 0.3) to get 5.88 m s⁻² (B).

items.stem: Inspect the first segment (0.0 s to 3.0 s) of the displacement–time plot for a motorized diffraction-slit carriage on an optical rail. What constant velocity does it have in this interval?
items.workedSolution: At t = 0.0 s, s₀ = 9 m; at t = 3 s, s₁ = 37 m. Velocity v = Δs / Δt = (37 − 9) / 3 = 9.33 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts initial position s₀ = 9 m to obtain v = (37 − 9) / 3 = 9.33 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: A student plots current I (y-axis) against potential difference V (x-axis) for a uniform manganin wire of length 2.00 m and cross-sectional area 8.00 × 10⁻⁸ m². The straight line of best fit passes through the origin and the point (6.00 V, 0.500 A). What is the resistivity of the manganin?
items.workedSolution: Gradient m = ΔI / ΔV = 0.5000 A / 6.000 V = 0.08333 A V⁻¹. Since gradient = 1/R, R = 1/m = 12.00 Ω. Therefore ρ = R A / L = 4.800 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Uses R = 1 / gradient and ρ = R A / L to obtain 4.80 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: During a mechanics practical, a beryllium-copper instrument spring follows the linear force–compression trace up to 1.0 m and subsequently accelerates a 0.5 kg block from rest across a frictionless bench.
items.workedSolution: (a) k = 90 / 1 = 90.0 N m⁻¹. (b) Elastic energy E_p = ½(90)(1) = 45.0 J. (c) Launch speed v = √(2(45.0)/0.5) = 13.4 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies k as the gradient ΔF / Δx.
Obtains k = 90.0 N m⁻¹.
Uses triangular area ½Fx.
Obtains E_p = 45.0 J.
Equates ½(0.5)v² to stored elastic energy from (b).
Obtains v = 13.4 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Inspect the constant-gradient reversal stage from t = 6.0 s to t = 9.0 s for a magnetic-levitation shuttle pod moving on a horizontal vacuum test guideway. What signed acceleration acts over this stage?
items.workedSolution: Between t = 6 s and t = 9 s, velocity changes from +16 m s⁻¹ to −8 m s⁻¹. Acceleration a = Δv / Δt = (−8 − 16) / (9 − 6) = -8.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates Δv / Δt = (−8 − 16) / (3) = -8.00 m s⁻² (D).

items.stem: Refer to the force–time profile of a pulsed ion-beam firing on a Hall-effect thruster test rig of mass 2.0 kg (initial momentum 6.0 kg m s⁻¹). By how much does its speed increase over the 0.8 s pulse?
items.workedSolution: Impulse J = area under F–t trapezium = ½(0.8 + 0.4)(50) = 30.0 N s. Speed increase Δv = J / m = 30.0 / 2 = 15.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes J = 30.0 N s and Δv = J / 2 = 15.0 m s⁻¹ (A).

items.stem: The graph shows the I–V characteristic recorded for an amber LED in an optics rig in an NCUK laboratory investigation, with current plotted on the vertical axis and potential difference on the horizontal axis. At the highlighted operating point, V = 2.20 V and I = 20 mA.
items.workedSolution: (a) R = V / I = 110.0 Ω ≈ 110 Ω. (b) connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the component and reverse the supply connections for negative readings. (c) conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.

markScheme.criterion: Substitutes operating-point values into R = V / I (converting mA to A if needed).
Correct static resistance 110 Ω.
Specifies potential divider (or variable supply) with series ammeter and parallel voltmeter.
Includes a series protective resistor and reversing supply connections for negative voltages.
Correctly describes how resistance changes across the graph.
Correct microscopic explanation: conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.

parts.prompt: Calculate the static resistance of the component at the highlighted operating point.
workingSteps: Recall that static resistance at a point is R = V / I (not the inverse of the local tangent).
Substitute V = 2.200 V and I = 0.02000 A to obtain R = 110.0 Ω ≈ 110 Ω.

parts.prompt: Describe the circuit arrangement and experimental procedure used to obtain a complete I–V characteristic safely across positive and negative potential differences.
parts.expectedAnswer: To obtain the full characteristic safely, connect a potential divider with a series protective resistor an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel across the component and reverse the supply connections for negative readings.
workingSteps: Use a potential divider to vary potential difference smoothly from zero while limiting excessive current with a protective resistor.
Measure current with a series ammeter, potential difference with a parallel voltmeter, and reverse the supply leads for negative polarity.

parts.prompt: Explain the physical shape of the I–V characteristic in terms of charge carriers and resistance.
parts.expectedAnswer: The curve shows that the component conducts sharply above the forward threshold voltage and has very high resistance in reverse bias.
workingSteps: Link the changing ratio of potential difference to current directly to the microscopic conduction mechanism.

items.stem: The graph shows how charge Q and potential difference V vary as an ignition-coil capacitor is charged uniformly from zero up to Q = 6.40 mC at V = 20.0 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates. (b) C = Q / V = 320 μF. (c) Triangular area E = ½ Q V = 0.06400 J ≈ 0.0640 J.

markScheme.criterion: States charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.
Correct capacitance 320 μF.
Recognises triangular area E = ½ Q V and converts mC to C.
Correct stored energy 0.0640 J.

parts.expectedAnswer: Capacitance is the charge stored per unit potential difference across the plates.

parts.prompt: Deduce the capacitance of the capacitor from the graph in μF.
Determine the electrical energy stored in the capacitor using the shaded triangular area under the graph.
workingSteps: Because V increases linearly from 0 to V_max as charge builds up, energy stored equals the triangular area E = ½ Q V.

items.stem: Over an interval of 6.0 s, a deep-sea winch capsule (initial velocity 9.0 m s⁻¹ upward) follows the plotted acceleration profile. What velocity does it have when t = 6.0 s?
items.workedSolution: Positive a–t area (0 to 3 s) = 24.0 m s⁻¹; negative area magnitude (3 s to 6 s) = 15.0 m s⁻¹. Net Δv = 24.0 − 15.0 = 9.00 m s⁻¹. Final velocity = 9 + (9.00) = 18.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Combines net signed area (9.00 m s⁻¹) with u₀ = 9 m s⁻¹ to obtain 18.0 m s⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: Evaluate the net work done by the resultant force on a cable-towed hydroplane model (mass 4.0 kg, initial speed 4.0 m s⁻¹) between x = 0.0 m and x = 12.0 m using the graph.
items.workedSolution: Forward work (0 to 10 m) = 120 J; resistive work (10 m to 12 m) = −4.00 J. Net work = 120 − 4.00 = 116 J.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts resistive triangle (4.00 J) from positive trapezium (120 J) to get 116 J (D).

items.stem: Along a horizontal guideway, a frictionless puck on an air table of mass 0.8 kg moves in a fixed direction. Its momentum–time graph shows an impulse stage from t = 1.0 s to t = 5.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resultant force F = Δp / Δt = (7.2 − 1.6) / (5 − 1) = 1.40 N. (b) Net work W = ΔE_k = (7.2² − 1.6²) / (2 × 0.8) = 30.8 J.

markScheme.criterion: Identifies resultant force as gradient Δp / Δt of the p–t graph.
Obtains F = 1.40 N.
Relates net work to ΔE_k = (p₂² − p₁²) / (2m).
Substitutes p₁ = 1.6 kg m s⁻¹, p₂ = 7.2 kg m s⁻¹, and m = 0.8 kg.
Obtains W = 30.8 J.

items.stem: Total circuit resistance R (including lead resistance R₀) is plotted against geometric ratio L / A up to 250.0 m⁻¹ for a germanium crystal prism. Calculate the electrical resistivity ρ.
items.workedSolution: Since R = ρ(L / A) + R₀, resistivity ρ equals the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A) = (32 − 8) / 250 = 0.0960 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: Subtracts intercept R₀ = 8 Ω to obtain ρ = (32 − 8) / 250 = 0.0960 Ω m (A).

items.stem: A variable load resistor is connected across a zinc-carbon dry cell, and the terminal potential difference V is plotted against current I up to 2.0 A. According to V = ε − Ir, what is the signed gradient of this graph?
items.workedSolution: At I = 0.0 A, V = ε = 7 V; at I = 2 A, V = 3.4 V. Gradient = (3.4 − 7) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (equal to −r).

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates (3.4 − 7) / 2 = -1.80 V A⁻¹ (C).

items.stem: A capacitor in a timing delay module discharges through a 50 kΩ resistor. The linear plot of ln(V / V) against time t has a vertical intercept of 2.485 and passes through (60 s, 0.485). What is the initial potential difference V₀ across the capacitor at t = 0?
items.workedSolution: Since ln(V) = −t/τ + ln(V₀), the vertical intercept is ln(V₀) = 2.485. Taking the exponential gives V₀ = e^(2.485) = 12.00 V ≈ 12.0 V.

markScheme.criterion: Extracts linearized graph parameters accurately to obtain 12.0 V.

items.stem: At t = 0.0 s, a canal lock towing locomotive rests at a position 25.0 m ahead of a lock-gate reference mark. The velocity–time graph shows its forward motion over 10.0 s, with uniform braking applied from t = 7.0 s until t = 10.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Trapezium area Δx = ½(10 + 5)(16) = 120 m. (b) Final distance from datum = 25 + 120 = 145 m. (c) Mean speed = 120 / 10 = 12.0 m s⁻¹. (d) Braking acceleration = (0 − 16) / (10 − 7) = -5.33 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Identifies distance travelled as the area under the v–t trapezium.
Obtains Δx = 120 m.
Adds 25 m offset to obtain 145 m.
Divides distance travelled from (a) by 10 s.
Obtains mean speed = 12.0 m s⁻¹.
Obtains braking acceleration = -5.33 m s⁻².

parts.prompt: Calculate the distance travelled during the 10.0 s journey.
workingSteps: Distance equals the trapezium area under the v–t curve.

Determine the mean speed over the 10.0 s run.
Calculate the acceleration between t = 7.0 s and t = 10.0 s.

items.stem: Engineers test a cross-linked elastomer strip under axial tension up to strain 0.5, recording an initial linear elastic regime between zero strain and 0.25.
items.workedSolution: (a) Young's modulus E = 180 / 0.25 = 720 MPa. (b) Energy per unit volume = ½(0.25)(180) + ½(180 + 260)(0.25) = 77.5 MJ m⁻³.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates initial gradient σ / ε up to ε = 0.25.
Obtains E = 720 MPa.
Identifies work per unit volume as total area under the σ–ε graph.
Splits area into initial triangle plus upper trapezium.
Obtains 77.5 MJ m⁻³.

items.stem: Refer to the linearized Coulomb graph of balance reading F against r⁻² (up to 16.0 m⁻²) recorded using charged copper electrodes on a laser-deflection cantilever.
items.workedSolution: (a) At r⁻² = 0, systematic tare offset F₀ = 0.120 N. (b) Gradient = (1.16 − 0.12) / 16 = 0.0650 N m².

markScheme.criterion: Reads intercept F₀ = 0.120 N.
Evaluates ΔF = 1.16 − 0.12 using intercept from (a).
Divides ΔF by 16 m⁻² and states correct unit N m².
Obtains 0.0650 N m².

items.stem: An electronics technician logs potential difference V against current I from zero to 1.2 A across a vacuum-tube heater filament.
items.workedSolution: (a) At I = 1.2 A, V = 12.6 V. (b) Static resistance R = V / I = 12.6 / 1.2 = 10.5 Ω (the upper segment gradient 18.0 Ω is ΔV / ΔI, not R).

markScheme.criterion: Reads V = 12.6 V at I = 1.2 A.
Selects R = V / I rather than local segment gradient ΔV / ΔI.
Substitutes V = 12.6 V and I = 1.2 A.
Obtains R = 10.5 Ω.

items.stem: To bound gradient uncertainty in a thermocouple electromotive-force test, a student plots the shallowest line of worst fit through the error-bar extremes between 1.0 K and 5.0 K.
items.workedSolution: (a) At 5 K, y₂ = 17.0 mV. (b) Worst-fit gradient = (17 − 5) / (5 − 1) = 3.00 mV K⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Reads y₂ = 17.0 mV.
Reads y₁ = 5 mV at x₁ = 1 K and forms Δy / Δx.
Subtracts x₁ = 1 K in the denominator (5 − 1).

parts.prompt: Read from the graph the thermal emf coordinate at 5.0 K on the worst-fit line.
workingSteps: At x₂ = 5 K, the line reaches y₂ = 17.0 mV.

parts.prompt: Calculate the gradient of this shallowest line of worst fit between 1.0 K and 5.0 K.
workingSteps: Read lower vertex y₁ = 5 mV at x₁ = 1 K.

items.stem: A student investigates a rigid nitrogen gas thermometer and plots the suppressed-origin graph shown, with vertical error bars of ±1.8 kPa. Two widely separated coordinates on the line of best fit are (25.0 °C, 115.9 kPa) and (85.0 °C, 140.8 kPa). The steepest straight line still passing through all error bars has gradient 0.3475 kPa K⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) m_best = (140.8 − 115.9) / (85.0 − 25.0) = 0.4150 kPa K⁻¹ ≈ 0.415 kPa K⁻¹. (b) Δm = |0.3475 − 0.4150| = 0.0675 kPa K⁻¹. (c) A suppressed origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly substitutes large-triangle coordinates (140.8 − 115.9) / (85.0 − 25.0).
Obtains best-fit gradient = 0.415 kPa K⁻¹ with correct compound SI unit.
Calculates Δm = |m_worst − m_best| = 0.0675 kPa K⁻¹.
States that a false origin expands the plotted data to fill more than half of the grid improving reading precision.

items.stem: The Cartesian plot shows experimental (V, I) data and the straight line of best fit for a uniform constantan wire of length 1.50 m and cross-sectional area 5.90 × 10⁻⁸ m². The line of best fit passes through the origin and reaches I = 0.640 A at V = 8.00 V.
items.workedSolution: (a) Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area. (b) Gradient = 0.08000 A V⁻¹, so R = 1 / gradient = 12.5 Ω. (c) ρ = RA/L = 4.917 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.92 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area.
Correctly specifies all quantities (or notes constant temperature / material property).
Computes large-triangle gradient m = ΔI/ΔV = 0.0800 A V⁻¹ and takes its reciprocal R = 1/m.
Correct wire resistance R = 12.5 Ω.
Substitutes R, A, and L correctly into ρ = RA/L.
Correct resistivity 4.92 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m with unit Ω m.

parts.prompt: Define the electrical resistivity of a material.
parts.expectedAnswer: Electrical resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross sectional area, where resistance, cross-sectional area, and length are measured for a uniform specimen at constant temperature.
workingSteps: State the definition in terms of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area.
Identify that resistivity is an intrinsic property of the material at constant temperature.

parts.prompt: Determine the resistance of the wire from the gradient of the I–V line of best fit using a large triangle.
workingSteps: Because I is on the vertical axis, R = 1 / m = 12.50 Ω ≈ 12.5 Ω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the resistivity of the alloy, stating the appropriate SI unit.
workingSteps: Evaluate ρ = 4.917 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m ≈ 4.92 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m.

items.stem: Refer to the Hooke's-law force–extension line for an optical-mount preload spring. What work is done in stretching it from x = 0.0 m to x = 1.0 m?
items.workedSolution: Elastic potential energy equals the triangular area under the F–x line: E_p = ½ F x = ½(70)(1) = 35.0 J.

markScheme.criterion: Computes triangular area ½(70)(1) = 35.0 J (D).

items.stem: The graph displays how the velocity of a seismic actuator test sled on a low-friction hydraulic guide varies with time over 20.0 s. Positive velocity corresponds to motion in the positive x-direction, and direction reversal occurs during the linear ramp between t = 10.0 s and t = 15.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Zero-velocity crossing is at t = 13.75 s. Positive area = 281 m and unsigned negative area = 56.3 m, giving total distance = 338 m. (b) Net displacement = 281 − 56.3 = 225 m; average velocity = 225 / 20 = 11.3 m s⁻¹. (c) Acceleration = (−10 − 30) / (15 − 10) = -8.00 m s⁻².

markScheme.criterion: Finds zero-crossing t = 13.75 s and evaluates both unsigned areas (281 m and 56.3 m).
Obtains total distance = 338 m.
Subtracts areas for net displacement (225 m) and divides by 20 s.
Obtains average velocity = 11.3 m s⁻¹.
Obtains acceleration = -8.00 m s⁻² including negative sign.

items.stem: A force transducer logs a 2.5 s pulsed ion-beam firing acting forward on a Hall-effect thruster test rig (mass 3.0 kg), which had momentum 9.0 kg m s⁻¹ at t = 0.0 s.
items.workedSolution: (a) Impulse J = ½(2.5 + 1.5)(46) = 92.0 N s. (b) Final momentum p_f = 9 + 92.0 = 101 kg m s⁻¹. (c) Speed increase Δv = 92.0 / 3 = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: Computes impulse from the trapezium area under the F–t curve.
Obtains J = 92.0 N s.
Adds 9 kg m s⁻¹ to obtain 101 kg m s⁻¹.
Divides impulse from (a) by 3 kg.
Obtains Δv = 30.7 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: The I–V characteristic graph for a headlamp tungsten bulb highlights an operating point where V = 9.00 V and I = 1.20 A. What is the static resistance of the component at this operating point?
items.workedSolution: Static resistance at any point on an I–V graph is R = V / I = 9.000 V / 1.200 A = 7.500 Ω ≈ 7.50 Ω.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates R = V / I accurately to obtain 7.50 Ω.

items.stem: The charging graph for a power-bank smoothing cell is a straight line from the origin to Q = 4.00 mC at V = 16.0 V. What is the capacitance of the capacitor?
items.workedSolution: Convert Q = 4 mC = 4.000 × 10⁻³ C. Capacitance C = Q / V = 2.500 × 10⁻⁴ F = 250 μF.

markScheme.criterion: Correctly converts mC to C and obtains 250 μF.

items.stem: At t = 0.0 s, a centrifuge carrier pod moves tangentially forward with an initial velocity of 4.0 m s⁻¹. The graph shows how its acceleration varies with time over 10.0 s (tangentially forward positive).
items.workedSolution: (a) Maximum speed occurs when acceleration crosses zero from positive to negative at t = 5.00 s. (b) Positive area = 28.0 m s⁻¹, giving v_max = 4 + 28.0 = 32.0 m s⁻¹. (c) Negative area magnitude = 16.0 m s⁻¹, so v_final = 32.0 − 16.0 = 16.0 m s⁻¹.

markScheme.criterion: States t = 5.00 s.
Evaluates positive area up to 5 s (28.0 m s⁻¹) and adds u₀ = 4 m s⁻¹.
Obtains v_max = 32.0 m s⁻¹.
Subtracts negative area (16.0 m s⁻¹) from v_max.
Obtains final velocity = 16.0 m s⁻¹.

items.stem: Force-transducer and encoder data for a warehouse pallet shuttle (mass 5.0 kg, speed 6.0 m s⁻¹ at x = 0.0 m) are plotted over a 20.0 m straight track.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates positive (276 J) and negative (−12.0 J) areas.

Uses ½mv² = ½(5)(6²) + W.
Obtains v = 11.9 m s⁻¹.
Divides net work by 20 m to get 13.2 N.

parts.prompt: Calculate the net work done on the 5.0 kg object between x = 0.0 m and x = 20.0 m.
workingSteps: Positive area (0 to 16 m) = ½(16 + 7)(24) = 276 J; negative area (16 m to 20 m) = −½(4)(6) = −12.0 J.

parts.prompt: Calculate its speed at x = 20.0 m.
State the mean resultant force over the 20.0 m displacement.

items.stem: The graph displays the linear momentum of a frictionless puck on an air table (mass 0.8 kg) against time. What resultant force acts on it between t = 2.0 s and t = 5.0 s?
items.workedSolution: By Newton's second law, F = Δp / Δt = (6.4 − 1.6) / (5 − 2) = 1.60 N.

markScheme.criterion: Evaluates F = Δp / Δt = (6.4 − 1.6) / (3) = 1.60 N (C).

options.distractorRationale: Computes the secant ratio p₂ / t₂ from the origin, ignoring both initial momentum p₁ and start time t₁.

options.label: B
options.distractorRationale: Multiplies Δp by Δt instead of evaluating the rate of change of momentum Δp / Δt.

options.label: D
options.distractorRationale: Divides Δp / Δt by mass m, obtaining acceleration rather than resultant force.

items.stem: To determine the resistivity ρ of a polypyrrole conductive polymer film despite probe and lead resistance R₀, a student plots total measured resistance R against the ratio L / A from 0.0 m⁻¹ to 400.0 m⁻¹.
items.workedSolution: (a) Vertical intercept R₀ = 8.00 Ω. (b) Resistivity ρ = (36 − 8) / 400 = 0.0700 Ω m.

markScheme.criterion: States R₀ = 8.00 Ω.
Identifies ρ with the gradient ΔR / Δ(L / A).
Subtracts R₀ = 8 Ω from 36 Ω before dividing by 400 m⁻¹.
Obtains ρ = 0.0700 Ω m.
